title: Competition and Resource Partitioning Review Test
description: Use resource-use models and controlled comparisons to explain competition and how differences in resource use can reduce overlap.

questions.prompt: Two fungi use sugars in the same fallen log. Could they compete even though neither chases the other?
questions.questionText: Two fungi use sugars in the same fallen log. Could they compete even though neither chases the other?
options: No; competition happens only among moving animals.
Yes; both may use a limited supply of organic material.
Only if they are different colors.
No; dead material is always unlimited.
questions.correctAnswer: Yes; both may use a limited supply of organic material.
questions.explanation: Competition can occur through depletion of shared material without direct fighting.

questions.prompt: A diagram shows A using rocky crevices and B using sandy burrows. What kind of separation is represented?
questions.questionText: A diagram shows A using rocky crevices and B using sandy burrows. What kind of separation is represented?
options: Use of different feeding times.
One organism eating another.
Use of different shelter locations.
Equal access to every resource.
questions.explanation: The model separates shelter use, not necessarily diet or timing.

questions.prompt: Plants with nearby neighbors gain 5 cm; matched plants alone gain 9 cm. What is the growth gap?
questions.questionText: Plants with nearby neighbors gain 5 cm; matched plants alone gain 9 cm. What is the growth gap?
options: 4 cm.
14 cm.
5 cm.
9 cm.

questions.prompt: Both fish species eat insect larvae. What evidence would best support actual competition for food?
questions.questionText: Both fish species eat insect larvae. What evidence would best support actual competition for food?
options: Both species were photographed underwater.
Larvae become scarce and each species grows better when the other's access is reduced under matched conditions.
Both have fins and live in the same lake.
Their names appear beside the same food in a book.
questions.correctAnswer: Larvae become scarce and each species grows better when the other's access is reduced under matched conditions.
questions.explanation: Shared use plus a measurable effect under resource limitation supports competition more strongly than diet overlap alone.

questions.prompt: One pollinator visits flowers in the morning and another later. Why might competition still occur?
questions.questionText: One pollinator visits flowers in the morning and another later. Why might competition still occur?
options: Different times always eliminate shared-resource effects.
The early visitor may deplete nectar faster than flowers replenish it.
Nectar cannot be a resource.
Both visitors must cooperate because they arrive separately.
questions.correctAnswer: The early visitor may deplete nectar faster than flowers replenish it.
questions.explanation: Time separation matters only in relation to resource availability and renewal.

questions.prompt: A resource-use table lists A: 15 bark insects, 5 ground insects; B: 6 bark insects, 14 ground insects. What does it show?
questions.questionText: A resource-use table lists A: 15 bark insects, 5 ground insects; B: 6 bark insects, 14 ground insects. What does it show?
options: Complete separation with no overlap.
Identical feeding patterns.
Different preferences with overlap in both food locations.
More total insects consumed by A.
questions.correctAnswer: Different preferences with overlap in both food locations.
questions.explanation: Each consumes 20 insects, but the distributions differ and both use both locations.

questions.prompt: Why is 'same habitat' insufficient to establish 'same niche'?
questions.questionText: Why is 'same habitat' insufficient to establish 'same niche'?
options: Every organism in a habitat has identical needs.
A niche describes only geographic coordinates.
Organisms in one place can use different foods, shelters, or times.
Habitats contain only one species.
questions.correctAnswer: Organisms in one place can use different foods, shelters, or times.
questions.explanation: A shared location does not establish identical resource use or interactions.

questions.prompt: A study compares crowded plants in small pots with isolated plants in large pots. Which factor complicates the claim about crowding?
questions.questionText: A study compares crowded plants in small pots with isolated plants in large pots. Which factor complicates the claim about crowding?
options: Plants have roots in both treatments.
Both groups can be measured in centimeters.
The experiment uses more than one plant.
Pot volume also changes soil and resource availability.
questions.correctAnswer: Pot volume also changes soil and resource availability.
questions.explanation: Crowding and pot volume vary together, so their effects are not separated.

questions.prompt: A finite token model contains 30 food pieces. A takes 18 and no food is added. What is the maximum left for B?
questions.questionText: A finite token model contains 30 food pieces. A takes 18 and no food is added. What is the maximum left for B?
options: 18 pieces.
12 pieces.
30 pieces.
48 pieces.
questions.explanation: The shared remainder is 30 - 18 = 12; it is not an independent supply.

questions.prompt: A shallow-rooted plant shares dry ground with a deep-rooted one. Which measurement best tests the proposed water partitioning?
questions.questionText: A shallow-rooted plant shares dry ground with a deep-rooted one. Which measurement best tests the proposed water partitioning?
options: Leaf color alone at one moment.
The length of each plant's common name.
Only the distance to the nearest road.
Water availability and root uptake at different soil depths.
questions.correctAnswer: Water availability and root uptake at different soil depths.
questions.explanation: The proposed mechanism concerns access at different depths, so measurements should address that access.

questions.prompt: Several species switch to the same remaining food during a shortage. What may happen?
questions.questionText: Several species switch to the same remaining food during a shortage. What may happen?
options: Partitioning must increase because foods are fewer.
Food becomes unlimited as diets converge.
All species stop using the shared food.
Resource overlap and competition may increase.
questions.correctAnswer: Resource overlap and competition may increase.
questions.explanation: A reduced range of foods can concentrate use of the same limited resource.

questions.prompt: A model shows one species using small seeds and another large seeds, but gives no seed quantities. What is a limitation?
questions.questionText: A model shows one species using small seeds and another large seeds, but gives no seed quantities. What is a limitation?
options: It describes separation but cannot establish how strongly either food supply limits growth.
It proves both species have equal populations.
It proves the two species never compete for any resource.
It establishes exact growth rates for both species.
questions.correctAnswer: It describes separation but cannot establish how strongly either food supply limits growth.
questions.explanation: Resource types alone do not provide availability, demand, or growth measurements.

questions.prompt: Plants alone gain 10 cm; with neighbors they gain 4 cm. After added minerals, plants alone gain 10 cm and neighbor-grown plants 8 cm. Which claim fits?
questions.questionText: Plants alone gain 10 cm; with neighbors they gain 4 cm. After added minerals, plants alone gain 10 cm and neighbor-grown plants 8 cm. Which claim fits?
options: Mineral addition reduced the neighbor-associated gap, but a difference remains.
Minerals had no possible effect.
Minerals eliminated the entire growth difference.
Neighbors became beneficial because 8 is greater than 4.
questions.correctAnswer: Mineral addition reduced the neighbor-associated gap, but a difference remains.
questions.explanation: The gap falls from 6 to 2 cm; that supports a contribution without proving a complete explanation.

questions.prompt: A seedling beneath a larger plant grows slowly even with moist soil. What other resource should be checked?
questions.questionText: A seedling beneath a larger plant grows slowly even with moist soil. What other resource should be checked?
options: The number of observers.
The label material.
Light reaching its leaves.
The species' alphabetical order.
questions.explanation: Adequate water does not exclude light limitation from shading.

questions.prompt: A report says partitioning guarantees coexistence forever. What correction is best?
questions.questionText: A report says partitioning guarantees coexistence forever. What correction is best?
options: It can reduce competition, but changing conditions and other shared resources still matter.
Partitioning prevents every kind of disturbance.
Partitioning makes populations independent of all resources.
Partitioning proves organisms intentionally cooperate.
questions.correctAnswer: It can reduce competition, but changing conditions and other shared resources still matter.
questions.explanation: Reduced overlap can support coexistence without guaranteeing permanence.
